title: $6,000 Senior Bonus Deduction Calculator 2026 (Age 65+)
description: Estimate your 2026 OBBBA senior 'bonus' deduction: $6,000 per person age 65+ ($12,000 married), with the 6% MAGI phase-out from $75k/$150k.
answerSnippet: The 2026 senior bonus deduction is an extra $6,000 per taxpayer age 65 or older ($12,000 for a married couple where both qualify). It phases out at 6% of MAGI above $75,000 single / $150,000 joint and runs through 2028.
intro:
The **One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA)** added a brand-new **'bonus' deduction for seniors** for tax years **2025 through 2028**: an extra **$6,000** for each taxpayer who is **age 65 or older** by the end of the year. A married couple where **both** spouses are 65+ can deduct **$12,000**.

This is **on top of** the regular standard deduction **and** the existing extra standard deduction that people 65+ already get. It is also available whether you **itemize or take the standard deduction**, and you need a **valid Social Security number**.

The catch is income. The deduction **phases out at 6% of the amount your MAGI exceeds the threshold** — **$75,000** for single filers, **$150,000** for married filing jointly. Enter your **filing status**, how many people on the return are **65+**, and your **MAGI** to see your deduction and the federal income tax it saves.
keyTakeaway: An extra **$6,000 per senior** (up to **$12,000** for a couple both 65+), stacked on the standard deduction and the existing age-65 add-on. It **phases out at 6%** of MAGI over **$75,000** (single) / **$150,000** (joint) — losing **$60 per $1,000** — and fully disappears near $175,000 (single) / $250,000 for a single-senior joint return. Temporary: **2025–2028**.

explanation:
## How the senior bonus deduction works

```
Base deduction = $6,000 × number of taxpayers age 65+
Phase-out      = 6% of (MAGI − threshold)
Threshold      = $75,000 single / $150,000 married filing jointly
Deduction      = max($0, base − phase-out)
```

The phase-out removes **$60 for every $1,000** of MAGI over the threshold (that is 6%). A single senior with a **$6,000** deduction loses it entirely at **$175,000** MAGI ($100,000 over the threshold × 6% = $6,000). A married couple with **one** 65+ spouse loses their $6,000 near **$250,000**; a couple where **both** are 65+ ($12,000) phases out closer to $350,000.

## It stacks with your other senior breaks

| Deduction | 2026 amount (illustrative) |
|---|---|
| Standard deduction (single) | $16,100 |
| Extra standard deduction, age 65+ | ~$2,050 |
| **New OBBBA senior bonus** | **+$6,000** |

The bonus is **in addition to** both of the first two, so a single 65+ filer can shelter substantially more income than in prior years.

## Requirements

- Be **age 65 or older** by the last day of the tax year.
- Have a **valid Social Security number** on the return.
- **MAGI** under the phase-out ceiling.
- Married filers generally must **file jointly** to claim it for both spouses.
- Available **whether or not you itemize**.

## Disclaimer

Educational estimate. Tax savings use your marginal rate and are approximate; the standard-deduction figures above are illustrative. It does not model state tax, the taxation of Social Security benefits, or credits. Confirm current amounts with the IRS and consult a tax professional.

faq.q: How much is the senior bonus deduction?
faq.a: **$6,000** for each taxpayer who is **age 65 or older**. A married couple filing jointly where **both** spouses are 65+ can deduct **$12,000**. It is a temporary OBBBA deduction for tax years 2025–2028.

faq.q: Is this on top of the standard deduction?
faq.a: Yes. The $6,000 bonus is **in addition to** the regular standard deduction **and** the existing extra standard deduction that filers 65+ already receive. You can claim it whether you itemize or not.

faq.q: At what income does the senior deduction phase out?
faq.a: It phases out at **6% of MAGI above $75,000** (single) or **$150,000** (married filing jointly) — a loss of **$60 per $1,000**. A single senior's $6,000 fully disappears at **$175,000** MAGI.

faq.q: Do I have to be 65 for the whole year?
faq.a: No. You qualify if you turn **65 by the last day of the tax year**. The IRS treats you as 65 on the day before your 65th birthday for this purpose.

faq.q: Does the deduction replace the tax break on Social Security benefits?
faq.a: No. It is a **separate income deduction**, not a change to how Social Security benefits are taxed. It simply lowers your taxable income if you are 65+ and under the income limits.

faq.q: Can a married couple with one spouse 65+ claim it?
faq.a: Yes — that couple claims **$6,000** (one qualifying senior). Only when **both** spouses are 65+ does the deduction reach **$12,000**.

faq.q: Do I need a Social Security number?
faq.a: Yes. A **valid Social Security number** must be on the return to claim the deduction. Married couples generally must file jointly to claim it for both spouses.

faq.q: Which years does the senior deduction apply to?
faq.a: Tax years **2025, 2026, 2027, and 2028**. It expires after 2028 unless Congress extends the provision.
